utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before my learned friend commences his cross-examination of the overnight witness, yesterday I tendered into evidence four Prosecution Exhibits marked P8, P9, P10 and P11. May I respectfully move that those four exhibits be admitted into evidence. Thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hajdarevic. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Yesterday, you answered questions put to you by the Prosecutor under a solemn oath. Today, you are going to answer questions put to you by the Defence counsel of Mr. Aleksovski, of course still under oath. Therefore, Mr. Mikulicic, the witness is now at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, learned colleagues of the Prosecution and Mr. Hajdarevic. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence has no questions to put to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Hajdarevic, you have completed your testimony. We thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who is the next witness, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my colleague Mr. Marchesiello will take over the next witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I will be taking as a witness Mr. Sulejman Kavazovic, who will be brought in court now. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Will you please read the statement which is presented to you. SULEJMAN KAVAZOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am sorry. Mr. Kavazovic, good morning. You are going to answer questions by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kavazovic. Do you feel comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can we start with your examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Will you please state to the court your full name, age and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Sulejman Kavazovic, I was born on 15th June 1969 in the village of Vrhovine in the municipality of Vitez in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How far is your birth place from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Vrhovine is about eight to nine kilometres away from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you state please your ethnic background, your nationality and your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak Muslim and a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Will you please outline for the court your educational background? Which school did you attend, starting from high school on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed my elementary schooling in the Dubravica school in Vitez. I completed transportation secondary school in Belgrade and then I completed the military academy as a deputy commander for the logistics and currently I am in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the rank of lieutenant, in charge of transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You did join the JNA. Did you serve in the JNA army and when and for how long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I served in Delnice in Croatia in 1988/1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Then did you have any experience as a civilian, in a civil profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I worked in Belgrade in a company called 4th July, Vostovac, as an officer for transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When did you leave Belgrade and in which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Belgrade on 18th February 1992, and the circumstances were that I was mobilised in the reserve units of the former JNA and I was afraid that I would be sent to the front-line in Slovenia or Croatia. My uncle who is in Belgrade and who is a policeman helped me to get out of Serbia and come into Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: At that time I understand you did return to Vitez. When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned to Vitez on 6th March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What did you do there? Did you start with any job or work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started to work in the secretariat for defence in the municipal headquarters. I was assigned to the post of policeman, and then in the municipal headquarters I was then appointed the chief for transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During that time, did somebody ask you, or offer you, or suggest to you to join the HVO and upon which assumptions; giving you which reasons for that possible choice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, and I would like not to mention his name, asked me to come to the HVO because the salary at the municipal headquarters was about 30,000 BH dinars. At that time you could still convert that money. In the HVO the salary would have been 400 Deutschmarks, which would have been a considerable difference. However, I refused that offer and I remained in the municipal headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: While living in Vitez and having joined the Territorial Defence, were you arrested between September 1992 and April 1993 by the HVO, and on how many occasions, if more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested by the Croatian Defence Council on three occasions. The first time I was arrested on 7th September 1992. I was taken to the Hotel Vitez and I was kept there -- I was held for about four hours. The second time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us stop at this point, since I have some questions to ask you about this first episode. You said it was on September 7th 1992. In which circumstances were you arrested? Were you arrested as a military or as a civilian? Were you dressed as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 7th September 1992, this was a Wednesday, it was a market day. I did not work that day, so I was in my civilian clothes and I was strolling in town. Around 1.30 pm, four members of the HVO detained me and took me to the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did they give any particular reason for the arrest in the beginning? Were they arresting Muslims randomly or in general, or were they aiming at specific individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I can offer my assumption. I think that the reason for my first arrest was because I was in charge of the transportation in the municipal headquarters in Vitez. I think that this was the reason I was detained for those four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This took place directly behind the Hotel Vitez, about 50 metres away from it. I was walking towards my apartment. First, two men approached me, asked me if I was Sulejman Kavazovic. I was taken aback, I said yes, I was, and he told me to follow him and I said "why", and he said, "you will get the explanation in the Hotel Vitez". When I started walking in the direction of the hotel, I realised I was detained, that I was going to be asked questions, I would have to answer questions and in the end I would be given the reasons for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which function did the Hotel Vitez have at that time? Was it still a hotel in the usual sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Hotel Vitez at that time was the command post of the Croatian Defence Council. It ceased to function as a place for civilians. Only certain people could walk in there as civilians, with the permission of the HVO. Other people did not have access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said you were interrogated by HVO military personnel. How many of them were there and did they belong to some special unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was questioned by three persons, one of them I know personally, his name is Vlado Santic. There were two other HVO soldiers there whom I did not know, they were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you know Vlado Santic from before? Which role did he have in the HVO, if it is to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Vlado Santic from before, but only -- knew who he was and knew him by sight. I never had come in contact with them. He was a policeman in the regular MUP of Yugoslavia, and this was all that I knew about him before I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what "MUP" means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The MUP means the Ministry of the Interior, so this is the regular police force of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What did they ask during your interrogation? What were they interested in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interested in certain things relating to the municipal headquarters and why I was in the municipal headquarters, why I was not in the HVO. I said that I had to be in the Territorial Defence headquarters because my people were there, and that if I were over there, maybe that would not be realistic because in the HVO, there were also only Croats, and that I was given a post there first, before the offer by the HVO. They asked me to explain what the Territorial Defence had in terms of its future plans, should there be any conflict between the HVO and the TO headquarters. I did not answer that question, because I had no idea. I told him that I was just involved in transportation, I was not involved in those matters. He also asked me whether there were any Mujahedin in Mahala. I said they did not because I had never seen them or I did not know that they were around, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. After how long were you released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released after about four hours. My command insisted -- in fact an agreement was reached between the HVO and the TO headquarters to release me. I asked for an explanation at the headquarters of the TO and nobody could give me one and I did not know, so nobody knew the reasons, because I was a civilian, I did not wear uniform, I had no insignia on me and I was detained by the members of the military formation, so I really did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will ask you some questions about your second arrest. When did it take place, do you remember it, and where were you actually arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember the arrest, it happened on 20th October 1992, I was arrested in front of the Hotel Vitez and the cinema called Slobodan Princip Selo. I was driving a van with permission and there was a permission between the HVO and the TO headquarters that we would be allowed to pass through. We had three or four vehicles at the headquarters, we had some equipment and some food and we were going to go to Stari Vitez and between the theatre and the Hotel Vitez, there were about ten members of the HVO, they had the solje and other weapons. There was Salih Omerovic there, who was then later killed in his apartment. Then they stopped us, they made us get out of the vehicles and then they detained us again in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. So I assume you were acting as a military in that moment, so you were in uniform, you were wearing your uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was wearing my uniform, it was a camouflage uniform, made of the tent material, canvas, because at first we did not have enough uniforms so we made them ourselves, so that was what I was wearing when I was arrested and taken to the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Were there other Muslim officers and/or soldiers held there as prisoners with you as you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no one there before us, so this man Salih and I were the first to arrive. However, after a while, while we were being questioned, and again I was questioned by Vlado Santic, then he ordered to the policemen to take us, so they took us to the ladies toilet, down in a bowling room, and we were locked up there and there was an armed guard who was guarding us there. We had received a guarantee from Sefkija Djidic, our commander, that we were free to pass through Vitez, the HVO had promised nobody would be mistreated so that we could reach Stari Vitez. However, we were the first who tried to pass through and we were arrested. In the logistics office where I worked, three other colleagues remained, my boss who was the chief for the logistics and two policemen. They stayed there, they were also captured then and they were brought over. However, Muhamed Patkovic, who was the chief of logistics, was beaten up, they beat him up and brought him down there and he joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you see him after he had been beaten on that occasion and how did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him personally, I even poured some water over him so that he would come to. His ear was split, he had bruises up here (indicates). We helped him to pull himself together down in the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened then, where were you taken from the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrest took place around 2.30, 3.00. We were detained in this Hotel Vitez, we were questioned for about half an hour. After that, they put us in this toilet down in the bowling room, and then they moved us to the civilian MUP of the HVO in a solitary. I do not know, but I heard that it was their prison of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please describe to the court the conditions of the place in which you were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This room -- we were eight or nine, I do not know exactly, there were also some people from Kotor Varos, Muslims. They were there before we arrived in this so-called black cell in the civilian MUP. It was dark, we did not have any light, we had nothing on the floor, we did not have a bench or anything, only in one corner there was a toilet bowl and that is where we relieved ourselves and that is where we stayed. So the conditions were very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there for three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: When were you released, in which circumstances? Were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was released on the fourth day in the morning, and there was an agreement which was reached between the HVO headquarters because there were some HVO members who were arrested by the TO and then the agreement was reached to exchange the prisoners of the HVO and the TO so in the morning around 10.00 I was exchanged. My communications officer from my headquarters arrived and he took me and they took me to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to turn your attention to the third arrest. When did it take place, and in which circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The third arrest happened in April 1993, on 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the court what happened on the morning of 16th April 1993. Where were you, and how did the day start for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, I was at my father-in-law's in his apartment, where I had spent the night with my wife, and about 5.10 or 5.15, I cannot recall exactly, a very powerful explosion woke me up, and I got up immediately and looked through the window, through the balcony, and I saw that things were not as they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I mean is that the moment I got up, I saw three or four groups of HVO soldiers, fully armed, under war gear, running towards a part of Stari Vitez. I realised that something was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was Stari Vitez the particular area of Vitez in which the TO were stationed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Stari Vitez was the place where the headquarters of the Territorial Defence was based and I worked there until 15th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us stay with 16th April. How did you spend that day? Did you hide in your father-in-law's apartment? Did you try to go away and reach your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, the 16th in the morning, when I was awakened by this powerful explosion, I looked through the window, saw these men running and I thought about it, seeing they were in complete war gear, that there must be a reason why they were running. So I realised that my position was not an easy one being a member of the Territorial Defence and that the whole of Vitez knew this. The part of the town where I was, that is where my father-in-law's apartment was, was under the control of the HVO. So I opened a part of the window, one of the panes of the window, and I looked around to see whether there was a chance for me to get out. But I saw that there were at least two HVO members standing and watching over each of the buildings. So if I had left through the window, one of them would have seen me, so I went back in and I spent all the time in the toilet or in the bedrooms, because on that day, 16th April, the Muslims were being rounded up from the buildings, they were put into cars and combi vehicles and taken towards the cinema, the hotel, the secondary school centre, the social accounting building, so I was afraid that someone might find me there because they knew I was a military policeman and that I was working in the TO headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go now to 19th April. Were you arrested in that occasion, on that day, and in which circumstances did it happen? Who did arrest you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 19th April 1993, my father-in-law's building, it was the turn of that building for the Muslims to be rounded up and detained in camps around Vitez. Since all the people in the building knew that I was there, both the Croats and the Muslims, no one had told anyone that I was there, but when this building's turn came to be cleansed of Muslims, I was in the apartment and suddenly my wife came in and said, "run as quickly as you can because they have come to collect you". (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) and my wife came up to him and told him I was in the apartment. He was surprised and wondered how come I was there and she said that we had been there for the past three nights and he told her, "all I can do to help him is to take him to the SDK", that is the social accounting building, "where I can help him and tell people not to hurt him, to take care of him and so on". So my wife came back and asked me whether I agreed and I said, "yes, I do not care. Obviously I have to give myself up, there is no point in hiding any more", and so he said he would come back in an hour's time, and he did come back with two military policemen and two civilian policemen. He put me in the van, me, my father-in-law and the other Muslims in that building, and we were driven off to the Vitez SDK building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation you found at the SDK? Had it been transformed into a detention place? How many, if Muslim, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation in the Vitez SDK building was very bad. A building that had three premises, the largest of which was 4 by 3 metres, and there were 62 civilians put up there. The age ranged from 12 to 62, the age of the detainees. We were piled up like sardines, we could not sleep, we could not move around, there was only a single toilet to 62 people, which is really below the minimum. We had no right to any visits at first. Later on, we were allowed to have visits. We could not ask for anything. In the morning, we got 125 grammes of fish and a quarter of a loaf of bread, and that was all we got in the first 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you stay at SDK, for how many days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the SDK for three days, until the 22nd , when I was taken by two military policemen and a driver, a Hungarian who was also a military policeman, and they took me to Rijeka to dig trenches and dugouts for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now Mr. Kavazovic, I am going to show you a map which has been already provided to the Defence, a military map, I think, of the area, of the Vitez-Busovaca area. May we have it numbered, please? Can you show it to the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document bears the number 12, it is exhibit number 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you see the map? Yes, thank you. Now, Mr. Kavazovic, can you show and sign with the marker which locality you have mentioned now, where you first were taken to dig trenches from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I was taken to dig trenches from Vitez to Rijeka, and I will mark the place called Rijeka where I was taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you sign it with an A, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Rijeka is being signed with A. How long did you stay there and for how long did you work trench digging in that place, in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Rijeka for about an hour, an hour and a half, not longer. I was digging trenches in the area between the HVO and the TO. I was exposed to fire, to very strong fire, and I stayed there for about an hour or hour and a half, not more. From there, I was taken to the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you please locate this place on the map, the place you refer to as the Bungalow. Where was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bungalow is a restaurant that was close to the village of Nadioci in Rasko Polje. It used to be a restaurant close to a bathing area and I shall mark it now. As the building as such cannot be seen, has not been marked on the map, I roughly circled the area where this restaurant, this Bungalow could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please mark the area with a B?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You say the Bungalow, you describe the Bungalow as a restaurant or in general a leisure place. Was it like that when you arrived there on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that place was no longer a recreational area, it was a place occupied by members of the HVO and by the Jokers, the special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please be more detailed about this Joker unit? In which kind of operation were they involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally do not know much about it, but as far as I know, it was a unit for special operations on front-lines when something needed to be captured, when an attack had to be carried out. They wore black uniforms, and what I found typical and important was that I recognised in the Bungalow Mr. Vlado Santic, who had interrogated me both the first and the second time in the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How did Santic react on seeing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Santic, when we arrived, lined us up on the terrace of this restaurant; he said, "line up, one next to the other", and I was the first. He addressed me, "so it is you again", those are the words he used. I did not say anything, I just shrugged with my shoulders and then he ordered five policemen and the policemen who had brought us there to put me and my colleagues in a car and to take me to Bralo, Miroslav Cicko's at Kratina and five or ten minutes later that is what they did. Five policemen got in with us and the same Madzar, Hungarian, was driving. They took us to Kratina, handed us over to Miroslav Bralo, or Cicko as he was known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now could you please sign the locality, the place corresponding to the name of Kratina, which I understand is a village within the hills. Do you know where -- can you show us where it is on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, I can show it to you, but let me first explain that Kratina is a Serb village with not more than five or six households and a Serbian chapel, and it lay just above Nadioci. The Serbs had moved out of that village in 1992 and it was close to Nadioci, so that it was later taken over by the Croats, so let me now mark Kratina where I was taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you mark the area with a C, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you. How was Bralo, the commander I assume, introduced to you on your arriving at Kratina and how did he look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was not introduced to us by anyone, but when we got there, this military police handed us over to Mladen Bralo, he said, "line them up here", we did, we stood one next to another in line and then he asked us whether we knew who he was. We said we did not, but I knew who he was. As a child, I used to go swimming at Rasko Polje. I never actually communicated with him, but I knew him by sight and I knew that they called him Cicko, but I did not know that his real name was Miroslav Bralo then. So I recognised him, whereas the others did not. He told us that his name was Miroslav Bralo, he said, "they call me Cicko", those were his words, he had a black bandanna, he had quite long hair, he had black leather gloves with the finger sections cut off, he had a Motorola, he wore a black uniform, and he asked whether any one of us knew how to cross ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kavazovic, first to go into this. Can I ask you, was there somebody else at his side that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Anto Furundzija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did he know you and did he tell you something on meeting you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time he did not say anything, he did know me. I and Anto Furundzija used to work together in the TO staff. Anto Furundzija was the commander of a platoon of 20 policemen in the TO staff because at first, in the beginning, in 1992, there were a certain number of Croats who were members of the TO staff. At the time, we were not just Muslims, but there were Muslims and Croats and even a small percentage of Serbs who were members of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Was Furundzija's attire the same as Bralo's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he also wore a black uniform and had a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Let us go back to this first meeting. You are saying that Bralo put you in a line and asked you to cross yourself; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he lined us up and he asked, "who knows how to cross himself?". I personally thought it over, I know how to do it the Serbian way because I spent quite a number of years in Belgrade and I knew how to cross myself in the Orthodox way, but I did not know how the Croats did it. Then a member who was with us, Mirsad Ahmic, he raised his hand and he said, "I know how to cross myself". He said, "you will go from one to the other and you will explain to each one of them how they should cross themselves", and he started with me, explaining out loud, "in the name of the father, the son, the holy spirit, amen", and then all of us had to cross ourselves like that and then when we did it he told us all, "now shout out loud these same words and cross yourself", and we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did somebody in that occasion make any mistake, and with what consequences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. While crossing himself, somebody called Jasmin Cengalovic, he was a gypsy, a Romany, and he got the order of the words wrong and then Mladen Bralo took a pickaxe, he lent it against his forehead, he cursed his balija mother and he said, "if you make a mistake now, I will cut your head off". I do not know whether it was out of fear or simply due to good luck, he managed to cross himself correctly and he said, "luckily you did it right".

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Kratina, and what you did during those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the 22nd at about 3.00, when I got to the Bungalow I was at Kratina by 4.00, until the 30th, I think, I do not know exactly, or maybe the 29th I stayed at Kratina. I was working, I had to do heavy manual labour, dig trenches, we carried planks, we roofed dugouts, we did digging mainly in areas exposed to fire where they could not do the work, we had to do it, under very strong fire of both sides, that is the HVO and the TO, they were exchanging fire and we were digging trenches between them, so that we worked from early morning until late into the night, sometimes even during the night until 2.00 or 3.00. During my stay in Kratina, I am a vegetarian and I do not eat meat or fish, but I was, of course, afraid for my life and I think it was the 28th, the day I was transferred to Busovaca, digging into a rock my palms were bloody from blisters and at one point I told a colleague of mine, "I cannot go on" and I fell, I lost consciousness. I fainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Can you stop a moment. Who asked you to dig into that rock, and which kind of tools did you have to dig into the rock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what his name was, I think he was one of the commanders, he must have been a commander when he was issuing orders. He gave us a pickaxe, I do not know how to explain it, a pickaxe which has a pointed end and we had to hit the rock with it, with the pick, but, of course, you could not do anything with it. Five of us took turns doing it, but I was the one who had to work hardest, because whenever he came up, he said, "why are you not working?", so I took the pickaxe and I hit the rock with it in their place, even, and I kept on working. I had to eat the fish, even though I could not stand it and I had great problems with my digestion and that is when I fainted about 4.00 in the afternoon, I do not know whether it was the 28th or the 29th exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I had fainted -- I fell into a coma, I woke up at Busovaca in the emergency ward. When I came to, I looked up, left and right, and I saw that there was a soldier of the HVO next to me, he had a shaven head and there were two nurses dressed in white and I had an infusion attached, an IV attached. I saw my colleagues, Jasmin Cengalovic and another one with me, and they were put into the van with me to accompany me to the emergency ward, and I asked them, "could anyone explain to me, what is this and where am I?". But one of the nurses, she was very beautiful, and she asked me how I was, whether I felt better. I just said that my arms were hurting and I could not stand up and that my head was hurting very bad and she told me that I had muscle cramp, probably from all that hard physical work and the stress I was exposed to. She said I was not to worry and that everything would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Where were you taken then from Busovaca, from that medical facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After about an hour, when I had recovered and I had received the intravenous drip and when I came to a little, the military police van came, the same one that was driving us all the time with the driver Madzar. I did not have a seat and I could not stand, so I held on to the roof and I was taken to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: What time was it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This may have been about 5.10 or 5.15 in the afternoon, before dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Who did receive you at that camp? Were you registered or did you receive some sort of -- was your name written down by some official in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one received us in the camp. We were taken there, the driver Madzar went in and said that we would stay there probably until the next morning or the day after, that he would come to pick us up with the van. I was taken over by a soldier of the HVO, I do not know his name, and he escorted us through a small corridor, then another corridor and then they put me up in a room with the number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Now Mr. Kavazovic, I am going to show you an aerial photograph of Kaonik camp. Can we have it numbered, please? Show it to the Defence as well, please. I think the Defence already has a copy of that. Do you recognise the area? Have you given a look at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Do you recognise the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please mark with a marker the building that you were brought into.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Will you sign it with the letter A, please? Mr. Kavazovic, you said you were taken into building number 5. Was this actually the number of the building, or do you connect this number -- this is something that belongs to any other source? Was it building with the number 5 on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This building I called this building number 5. Counting the buildings that are in the compound, and I am going to show you presently, I numbered it as 5, so it was my own marking. I do not know if that is really building number 5. I used it for my own marking. This would be building number 1, next to it would be number 2 and then 3, 4, 5 (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you please sign each building with a different, starting with B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: So you marked the buildings respectively, the building you were detained in with letter A and the surrounding buildings with letters B, C, D and E. Let us go to building A. Was it divided into cells? How can you describe the interior of that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of this building marked with A there is a balcony, which on one of its sides has a staircase and that is an entrance and then from this entrance you enter the building, so inside the building. You pass through a small hallway, maybe it is one or two metres long, and then you reach another hallway and in this hallway are these rooms where we were put up. The first room is on the right-hand side. On the left-hand side is a toilet and then there would be rooms 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, and on the other side 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Which was the aspect of the cell you were put into. How many of you were in the same cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The cell where I was placed would have been 3 by 3 or 3 by 2, something like that, maybe 3 by 4 I am not sure, because I could not see, it was dark. But it was not large. We were three in this cell where I was, myself, Adnan Pilic and there was a Croatian man, I think his name was Zeljko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How long did you remain at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Kaonik for two nights; that is I spent that night and the following night and on the third day in the morning, I was taken to the SDK building in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: During those two nights and three days, were you forced to perform any work while at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the next day I went out to load up some ten sandbags into a truck and that was all that I was forced to do in terms of any labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you see something unusual while loading?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The corner I could see between buildings B and C, there was a road between buildings A and C, and there I saw -- I am going to show it here, where I saw a military truck belonging to the HVO, where some crates were being loaded. I am also going to show the spot where I loaded the sand, sandbags, I do not know what it was for, what its purpose was. I could assume what its use may have been, but this is what I am going to show now. Here at this intersection, that is where I was loading this truck, it was a small truck (indicates). There were sandbags and there was a man who ordered us, he was inside, he was a guard. This was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you mark that spot with the letter F, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Thank you, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next I am going to show where the truck was, where some green crates, some military crates were being loaded. This was the building, marked with C. This is where the truck was, which was loading ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Could you mark that point with letter G, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Witness marks map).

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You said that they were loading a truck with ammunition, is this your evaluation of the scene, is it something that you imagined? Will you please be more specific on that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my assumption. There were green military crates being loaded on to this truck. It could not have been food, it could only have been some kind of ammunition. I do not know this for certain, but I assume it was some kind of ammunition. There were always one or two trucks there, I heard that later from my colleagues after we were exchanged and after we were in Zenica, a colleague of mine said there was always a truck there and it was always transporting some things, so I -- that is what I heard, but I saw that on that day, I saw this truck being loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet the warden, the commander of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never met the gentleman, nor did I ever see him. Not only him, in fact it was only a single guard that I saw and I may not be able to recognise him. That is all with respect to the camp as a camp. I saw a colleague of mine during the breakfast time when I was going to the toilet, there was a father of a soldier of mine who served in Belgrade. When he saw me there at the toilet, he asked me what I was doing there, I said that I did not know and tears appeared in his eyes, because he was sad. He had a son my age, around my age, and that is all I saw in terms of the people that I knew or knew of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: You never heard the name of Zlatko Aleksovski during your stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never heard of the name Zlatko Aleksovski or any other name, because I spent very little time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: How and in which circumstances were you released, then? You were probably already told, but state please again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third day in the morning in Kaonik, this man Madzar came, the man who drove me around to dig trenches, he came with two policemen and myself and two colleagues of mine, Jasmin Cengalovic and Adnan Pilic, we were returned to the SDK building in Vitez, where we were to wait for the exchange, so we would go either in the direction in Zenica or Travnik, where we could continue to live our normal lives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I apologise for the interruption, are you about to finish or shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: I have no other questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that case, we are going to have a 20 minute break. Thank you. (11.15 am) (A short break) (11.45 am)

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: With your Honours' permission, before cross-examination starts, I would like to tender the two exhibits that have been shown to the witness into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, you are now going to answer questions from Defence counsel of Mr. Aleksovski. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. My name is Goran Mikulicic and I am Defence counsel for Zlatko Aleksovski. Good afternoon. Mr. Kavazovic, I will ask you several questions so please try to respond to them to the best of your recollection. You said that upon your return from Belgrade to Vitez you worked in the Territorial Defence headquarters, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that your salary was, if my memory serves me rightly, about 3,000 dinars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, 30,000 BH dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how much money that would have been converted into Deutschmarks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, maybe 70 or 80 German marks, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on three occasions altogether during these events you were arrested. On all three occasions, you were exchanged -- correction, the second and the third time. The first time it was only an interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time it was an information interview, but I was arrested, I was captured because I was in my civilian clothes, not in military clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kavazovic, when you say that you were exchanged, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what it entails, but I know when I was first arrested, that was an agreement between the then Territorial Defence and the HVO to let me go and under what circumstances that happened, I do not know. The second time I know that Stuart Anderson, the UN commander in Nova Bila, arranged for the exchange and I went from Vitez to Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, you use the word "exchange". Does that imply that on the part of the Territorial Defence, somebody was released as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that, because I did not see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Kavazovic, in the events relating to your release or exchange, was Mr. Aleksovski involved or did he have any participation in any of these events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony, you said that you were forced to perform certain physical tasks during trench digging in Kratina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zlatko Aleksovski there at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know Zlatko Aleksovski at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Did you hear from anyone --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not finish my question. When you were staying in Kratina or Rijeka, have you ever heard Zlatko Aleksovski's name mentioned at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately, these locations Kratina and Rijeka, how far are they from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, I really do not know that part around that area, around Kaonik, so do not hold me for this, but it is about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it is your best assessment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you spent two nights in Kaonik altogether?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any guards in the building where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two guards who were there all the time, whether they were changing that I do not know, because I was inside, but there were two guards in my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did these persons carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of them had an automatic rifle of a domestic make from Yugoslavia and the other one had a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were these persons dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on their uniforms which would identify them as belonging to a certain unit or rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see. I only saw the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you mentioned a person named Miroslav Bralo, called Cicko. You mentioned a person named Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, I am going to ask you a few questions about them. Do you know who Darko Kraljevic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Darko Kraljevic was the commander of HOS in the Vitez municipality. HOS stands for "Croatian Armed Forces".

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how this unit that you just mentioned was armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is difficult to say. They had rifles, for the rest I cannot speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about him as a person? Do you know anything about him that is characteristic of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what would be characteristic. I know that they wore the black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, I am asking you about the personality of Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that he liked to drink, he had a coffee bar, and he had a circle of his own men over whom he had command like Lujic and the young Kistra, so they obeyed his orders. That is what I know. For a while, he was taking medication because his mother was good friends with my mother-in-law and there was a problem once with him, because he threw everybody out of the apartment because he took a larger dose of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A larger dose of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, she just said that he came home and he was drunk and he took a larger dose. I do not know what the dose was of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, I am not going to ask you anything about Miroslav Bralo, in order to avoid repeating anything. I just want to sum up. Correct me if I am wrong, but you said you never saw Zlatko Aleksovski and that you did not know him, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the time when you were forced to perform labour duties, you never saw him or you never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence has no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCHESIELLO
utterances.text: No other questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Kavazovic, you have completed your testimony. The Tribunal wishes to thank you for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you too, your Honours. Thank you and goodbye. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence counsel would like to request permission to address the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any questions regarding this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours. We have no further evidence for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may address the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask my colleague Mr. Joka to address the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually I wished directly to speak to my learned colleagues on the other side of the court, with a request. At the beginning of the week, we submitted a motion for the provisional release of the accused. The Prosecutor was given a period of time by the Trial Chamber, we have no doubt that that period will be respected, but we do appeal to the Prosecution to respond to this motion as soon as possible so that we can receive the judgement of the Trial Chamber, also as soon as possible. That would be all, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not envisage any difficulty in complying with the time limit of eight days that was set by the Tribunal. That being the evidence for today, your Honours, I think that we have witnesses -- we are approaching witnesses for the next session, and sometimes it is a bit difficult to predict whether or not we need all the witnesses or less, so it is not always entirely precise until we get more into the case and realise how long each witness is going to take. We were a little short in our estimate today, but in any event, we could not have had more witnesses here because these were the only witnesses available to come at this time of year so hopefully on the next occasion we will be able to ensure that the full period of time that has been allocated will be filled up. As I say, it is not easy because it is not a good policy to bring witnesses here and not call them and then send them back and then bring them back again, that creates considerable stress on the witnesses and we try and avoid that. Sometimes our prediction can be a little inaccurate. That is the evidence so far for today. We understand I think the next date is 23rd to 26th. Your Honours, the only other thing -- perhaps the only other thing has just been mentioned to me. I had assumed that your Honours will respond to the application by the Defence for provisional release on the basis of the written material submitted, you would not be seeking oral submissions on that. If your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber understands perfectly that it is not possible to fill all the available time always, but in any event, I think that every effort has been made to begin this trial and to take advantage of the time available. Therefore, our next session will be from 23rd to 27th February, only in the morning, that is from 9.00 until 1.15 pm. The other session will be from 6th March all day, and afterwards the 23rd to 27th, only afternoon. Therefore the afternoon from 2.15 to 7.00 pm. That is the envisaged timetable until next March, when we expect to have a second courtroom. I do not know whether the Prosecution or the Defence have any comments to make at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, no comments from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have no comments, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are going to adjourn therefore for this week and we will meet again here on 23rd February. Have a nice weekend everyone and success in your work. Thank you. (12.05 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: on Monday, 23rd February 1998) 20 21 22 23 24 25
